issues.explanation: The profile omits both Triggers and Threat entirely, yet includes carrying a weapon and persistent on-guard appraisals. For a 60-year-old male with military trauma, these items are individually plausible, but together they imply an active current-danger/threat system that is not represented elsewhere in the selected nodes and sits poorly with the formulation, where Threat and Triggers are not linked to the active network.

issues.item: Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time
issues.explanation: 'I have to be on guard all the time' functions more like a live threat appraisal, but the formulation centers the case on a Negative Appraisals ↔ Memory ↔ Maladaptive Strategies loop, with Threat inactive. In the absence of any other threat-focused items, this item is the main source of incoherence.

issues.item: Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
issues.explanation: 'Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning' implies salient cue-driven triggering, but all Triggers edges are inactive and no Trigger items are selected. That does not by itself make triggered recall impossible, but combined with the otherwise appraisal/guilt/identity-focused formulation and profile, it is the least coherent memory item.

issues.item: Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
issues.explanation: This item is difficult to reconcile with the formulation because Threat is not otherwise represented in the self-report and all Threat-related edges are inactive. The rest of the profile is organized around guilt/identity loss and trauma memory, whereas constant threat scanning implies an active current-threat focus that is not supported by the selected Threat, Trigger, Appraisal, or Memory items. The avoidance items fit the military trauma context, but this hypervigilant checking behavior appears clinically disconnected from the rest of the profile.

vignette:
Frank is a 60-year-old man who has worked the same warehouse job for the last twenty years, a life of quiet routine that stands in stark contrast to the chaos that tore his youth apart. He has come to therapy at the urging of his partner, reporting decades of distress rooted in his service in Vietnam. The inciting event is a memory he has never been able to fully articulate. During a patrol in a dense jungle, his platoon was ambushed. The attack was sudden and overwhelming-a blur of noise, muzzle flashes in the green gloom, and the cries of his friends. He survived by diving into a ditch, where he lay motionless as the firefight raged and then fell silent. When he finally emerged, he was one of only three survivors in his platoon, surrounded by the bodies of men he considered brothers.

When the past intrudes on the present, it is not as a coherent story but as a sensory and emotional assault. Frank describes how the memory brings back the same raw terror he felt in that ditch, a physical certainty that his life is about to end. This terror is immediately followed by a wave of profound guilt, a feeling so potent it seems to curdle in his stomach. He has tried, on rare occasions, to explain it to his partner, but he finds he cannot find the words to describe what happened or the weight of having lived when so many others did not. The experience remains locked inside him, a silent horror film playing on a loop.

This visceral recall of the event consistently reinforces the dark conclusions he has drawn about himself and the world. Each time the terror and guilt resurface, it cements his belief that he is fundamentally damaged, a man who doesn't deserve the life he was given. He feels intense survival guilt, a conviction that it should have been him who died that day. This conviction sends him mentally back to the ditch, as if searching the chaotic sensory fragments of the ambush for an answer to the unanswerable question of why he was spared. In response to these terrifying memories, Frank has spent decades trying to outrun them. He assiduously avoids thinking about the event, changing the subject if anyone mentions the war and shutting down the television if a military documentary appears. This constant effort to suppress the past is his primary means of coping with the unbearable feelings the memories evoke.

Over time, these negative appraisals have become the lens through which he views his entire past, tainting even memories that should be neutral. The belief that he is a different, lesser person now makes him feel that the young man who went to war is a stranger he no longer recognizes. This sense of a fractured identity makes looking back at any part of his life feel painful and alien. Because he has come to believe the world is an irredeemably dangerous place and that he is permanently broken, he feels a desperate need to control his environment to prevent any reminders from breaking through. He refuses to go near the local VFW post, seeing it as a place saturated with the past he must avoid. Years ago, he threw out his old fatigues, and even now, the drab, olive-green of his work coveralls can feel uncomfortably heavy, a low-grade echo of the uniform he once wore.

This pattern of avoidance, meant to protect him, has only served to deepen his negative beliefs. By refusing to speak about his experiences, he has isolated himself, which strengthens his conviction that he is fundamentally alone and unknowable. The more he avoids places and thoughts connected to his past, the more powerful they seem, and the more fragile and incapable he feels in the present. At work, a loud bang from a dropped pallet can send a jolt of pure panic through him, and the subsequent shame he feels for this reaction in a mundane setting only confirms his belief that he is no longer the man he once was. The avoidance has become a cage, reinforcing the very appraisals that drive it.

It was after a car backfired on their street last month that his partner insisted he seek help. She found him frozen in the kitchen, pale and trembling, unable to speak. The fear in her eyes was more terrifying to him than his own. Frank has come to therapy not with any real hope of recovery, but with a deep weariness and the quiet fear that he has lost himself for good. He doesn't know who he would be without the guilt that has defined him for over forty years, and the thought of finding out is the most frightening prospect of all.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Negative Appraisals → Memory: The vignette does not describe how Frank's negative appraisals (e.g., 'I am damaged') influence or trigger his trauma memory.
  e.g. "The belief that she was permanently changed kept bringing her back to the moment it had happened, as if she needed to locate exactly where she had been lost."
  e.g. "Telling herself that she should have seen it coming made the memory more vivid and easier to find — it sat there waiting, proof of her failure."
  e.g. "The conviction that she was weak fed directly into the flashback, colouring it, making it worse: she wasn't just there again, she was there again and helpless."
